p: On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry under Brigadier General John Buford deployed along McPherson's Ridge west of Gettysburg. Buford recognized the strategic importance of the high ground and determined to hold it until infantry arrived.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 1, “McPherson Ridge” (The Battle Begins), paragraph 1 of 3

p: When Heth's Confederate division advanced down the Chambersburg Pike, Buford's dismounted troopers fought a delaying action from behind fence rails and earthworks. Their stand bought precious time for Reynolds' I Corps to arrive.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 1, “McPherson Ridge” (The Battle Begins), paragraph 2 of 3

p: General John Reynolds, one of the most respected officers in the Army of the Potomac, rode forward to direct the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Minutes later, he was killed by a Confederate sharpshooter — one of the highest-ranking Union officers to die in the battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 1, “McPherson Ridge” (The Battle Begins), paragraph 3 of 3

p: While the fighting raged on the Union left on July 2, Johnson's Confederate division attacked the right flank at Culp's Hill. Greene's New York brigade — only 1,400 men — held a mile of trenches against nearly 4,700 attackers through the night.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 10, “Culp's Hill” (The Overnight Fight), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Greene's men benefited from the solid earthworks they had constructed, firing from protected positions while Confederate attackers struggled uphill through dense woods in darkness. The fight continued sporadically through the night.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 10, “Culp's Hill” (The Overnight Fight), paragraph 2 of 3

p: At dawn on July 3, the XII Corps returned from Cemetery Ridge and launched a series of assaults to recover the lost trenches. The fighting continued for seven hours — the longest sustained engagement of the three-day battle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 10, “Culp's Hill” (The Overnight Fight), paragraph 3 of 3

p: In the fading light of July 2, Ambrose Wright's Georgia brigade achieved what no other Confederate force managed that day: they crested Cemetery Ridge and briefly reached the Baltimore Pike.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 11, “Cemetery Ridge” (Wright's Breakthrough), paragraph 1 of 3

p: "We were on the crest," Wright later wrote. "We had pierced the enemy's lines." But Posey's and Mahone's brigades, which were supposed to support Wright's flanks, failed to advance. Hit from three sides, Wright's unsupported men were driven back.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 11, “Cemetery Ridge” (Wright's Breakthrough), paragraph 2 of 3

p: Hancock rushed every available man to seal the breach. The crisis passed — but it showed Lee that the Union center could be broken. The observation would inform his decision to order Pickett's Charge the following day.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 11, “Cemetery Ridge” (Wright's Breakthrough), paragraph 3 of 3

p: At 3:00 PM on July 3, the survivors of the mile-long advance reached the stone wall at The Angle. Armistead, with his hat raised on his sword so men could see him through the smoke, called out: "Come on boys, give them the cold steel!"

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 12, “The Angle” (The High-Water Mark), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Armistead led approximately 150 men over the wall and reached Cushing's guns. Artillery Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing had remained at his battery despite being wounded twice, holding his intestines with one hand while commanding with the other. He was shot through the head at the moment of Armistead's breakthrough.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 12, “The Angle” (The High-Water Mark), paragraph 2 of 3

p: Armistead fell wounded at the guns. Told that his old friend Hancock was also wounded nearby, he asked that his watch and personal effects be delivered to Hancock with his regrets. Armistead died two days later.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 12, “The Angle” (The High-Water Mark), paragraph 3 of 3

p: While Pickett's Charge unfolded a mile to the west, JEB Stuart's cavalry attempted to reach the Baltimore Pike and strike Meade's rear. Four Confederate brigades — Hampton, Fitz Lee, Chambliss, and Jenkins — advanced toward the Union rear.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 13, “East Cavalry Field” (Stuart vs. Custer), paragraph 1 of 3

p: Gregg's Union cavalry division, reinforced by Custer's Michigan brigade, blocked the advance. The 23-year-old George Armstrong Custer charged Hampton's brigade at full gallop with the 7th Michigan, shouting "Come on, you Wolverines!"

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 13, “East Cavalry Field” (Stuart vs. Custer), paragraph 2 of 3

p: The collision of the two cavalry forces stopped Stuart cold. Hampton was wounded. By the time Pickett's Charge had failed, there was no longer any rear to strike. Stuart withdrew, and the East Cavalry Field action passed largely unnoticed amid the drama at The Angle.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 13, “East Cavalry Field” (Stuart vs. Custer), paragraph 3 of 3

p: At 1:07 PM on July 3, 1863, Confederate artillery opened the greatest bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere — 150 guns firing simultaneously at Cemetery Ridge. The cannonade lasted nearly two hours.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (map walkthrough)
p.short: Site walkthrough stop 14, “Pickett's Charge” (The Mile-Wide Advance), paragraph 1 of 3
